newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Outgoing HK Democrats toast outgoing governor.
newsitem.headline: Outgoing HK Democrats toast outgoing governor.

text.p: There was laughter, toasts and sea food as Democratic Party legislators due to lose their seats after the Hong Kong's handover to China bid farewell to the governor whose electoral reforms helped put them in office.
The Democratic Party, which dominated the popular vote in the September 1995 polls for the Legislative Council, held a farewell dinner on Friday for outgoing governor Chris Patten.

Patten and about 20 others gathered in an airconditioned glass booth at a restaurant in Hong Kong's Lei Yue Mun, reached through a warren of watery alleys lined with stalls selling fish, lobsters, eels and other sea food.
Party leader Martin Lee, recently back from a trip to North America where he warned of impending curbs on civil liberties in Hong Kong, made a speech, greeted by much laughter.
Then Patten, who in 46 days steps down as the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong, made a speech and toasted his hosts with a glass of beer.

The Democratic Party won 12 of the 20 directly-elected geographic constituency seats in Hong Kong's Legislative Council in 1995 polls. Five more won profession-based functional constituency seats and two were chosen by an electoral commitee, making the party the biggest in the 60-seat legislature.
But they will all be ousted when the council is replaced by the Provisional Legislature to be installed on July 1 after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty.

China has vowed to scrap the current legislature, saying the electoral reforms introduced by Patten, which resulted in the first fully elected council in Hong Kong's history, violated previous Sino-British agreements.
The Democrats in turn refused to participate when a 400-member China-backed committee chose the provisional legislature, which will seat many who lost to Democratic Party members in the 1995 polls.
